response:
I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care is essential, but non-digital options must stay for those who need them. In Wales, online booking has reduced phone queues and helped me arrange a quick appointment. I’ve had a video check for a routine anxiety concern, which saved a trip and got me a clear plan sooner. For those without internet or who prefer not to use apps, a reliable phone triage line and in-person slots should remain, with staff able to support digital access where possible.

I also welcome investment in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, community and mental health services together with social care and VCSE partners. A hub near us now offers a GP, district nurse, mental health link worker and a local charity under one roof, making triage faster and signposting smoother. It cuts travel for families and helps older residents stay independent.

Successful rollout will need privacy safeguards, staff training and ongoing digital literacy support to ensure no one is left behind.

Timely access would be most improved by targeted resources for communities facing the biggest barriers, accompanied by interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus active outreach in deprived and ethnic minority areas. In my area, language and digital barriers still slow GP bookings and mental health referrals. Funding dedicated interpreters at front desks and during triage, plus multilingual health information, would cut missed appointments and confusion about what help is available. Outreach workers who understand local gaps could help migrant and marginalised families know how to navigate services and access timely care. 

I also support expanding multidisciplinary teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to treat routine cases and free GPs to focus on complex needs. A practice nearby now uses a pharmacist-led review for repeat prescriptions and a physio for common musculoskeletal issues, which reduced GP wait times and improved patient satisfaction. Clear referral pathways and flexible booking (same-day slots, online triage) would further speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services while maintaining safety and continuity of care.

We disagree with expanding online booking and remote care without solid non-digital options; many in our area, especially elderly and disadvantaged, would be excluded. Instead invest in improved triage, simplified NHS111, and guaranteed same-day urgent slots with evening/weekend access.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we protected continuity of care and lengthened appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. A named GP or stable care team means the clinician knows my history, medicines and recent changes, reducing miscommunications and unnecessary trips back. In practice this would require longer slots—20 to 30 minutes—for people with multiple conditions or cognitive issues, and reliable follow-up after hospital discharge. 

Integrating community health professionals and mental health staff into primary care would also help. For example, an embedded mental health nurse can triage early, provide brief interventions, and coordinate with social care, reducing crisis turns and long waits elsewhere. 

Booking systems should reflect complexity: triage calls that schedule appropriate time, not just the first available slot. And we need flexible access—same-day slots when needed, with a clear path to longer appointments without stigma or delay. 

Adequate funding and workforce planning are essential, along with monitoring outcomes like fewer unplanned hospital visits and higher patient satisfaction.

In our area, improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will hinge on a smarter combination of triage, booking systems and care navigation, backed by a real expansion of community mental health teams. NHS111 is useful, but it often creates a delay when it routes urgent concerns through multiple steps. I’d like to see stronger clinical triage by trained clinicians, with same‑day GP or nurse appointments prioritised for urgent issues, and more reliable callback times. A real‑time online booking portal showing short-notice availability would help families avoid fruitless phone loops and reduce unnecessary A&E visits.

Practically, we need a single, simple patient journey: one update to a shared record, fewer repeated questions, and a dedicated care-navigation hub that explains the next steps and keeps patients out of duplication loops. If someone is told to undergo tests or referrals, the path should be streamlined, with clear timeframes and someone who can guide you through it rather than starting from scratch at each touchpoint.

On mental health, expanding community teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies would be transformative. In my circles, waiting weeks for counselling or crisis support is common; expedited access and parity with physical health services would reduce crises and hospital admissions. Investment to recruit staff and sustain services, plus 24/7 crisis lines and wider access to talking therapies, would make care more humane and effective for families and individuals alike.

To improve timely access, expand appointment slots by hiring more staff and extending hours, including evenings and weekends, and guarantee same-day urgent slots; also recruit internationally where needed and offer flexible work and wellbeing support to retain teams.

I’d prioritise changes that protect continuity of care and make time for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. In practice that means longer appointment times and a consistent clinician where possible, so care plans can be monitored without endless repeat visits. I’ve seen how a single short slot can leave someone with multiple conditions unsure what to do next; a longer initial consultation and guaranteed follow-ups would cut downstream demand and improve outcomes.

For mental health, expanding community teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies is essential. In my area, people wait too long for therapy, and crisis support is inconsistent. A joined-up, ring-fenced service that can offer rapid access, with integrated care plans alongside physical health services, would make a real difference and help parity with physical care.

Transport and premises are real barriers, especially in rural or mobility-limited contexts. I’d support mobile clinics, local outreach, and telehealth hubs that operate in community centers and GP practices. Incentives to recruit clinicians to hard-to-reach areas, subsidies for travel or parking, and better accessible premises would also help. A phased rollout with local pilots would let us learn what works where we live and scale up confidently.

I disagree that simply expanding training and co‑located hubs will quickly fix delays; it takes years to train new GPs and clinicians. We need immediate recruitment, cap on caseloads, and better funding for current services.

I welcome the government’s focus on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely and easier to access. In my area in England, there are real differences in how quickly people can get help, and those gaps fall hardest on people who are deprived, come from ethnic minority communities, or are newer migrants. I’ve seen neighbours and colleagues delay seeking care because the phone line is busy for hours, online booking is tricky to use if you don’t have reliable internet, or there simply aren’t convenient appointments offered when someone needs help the most. When language or cultural barriers get in the mix, the problem compounds. A friend who doesn’t feel confident speaking English told me she avoided making GP appointments because she was worried about a miscommunication and wasn’t sure how to find interpreters. A neighbour who has recently arrived in the country found it nearly impossible to access mental health support without someone to translate or explain the system. These aren’t just statistics; they’re real lived experiences that can lead to worse health outcomes over time.

If we’re serious about improving timely access, I think the changes should include the following, clearly funded and rolled out with local authority and NHS partners:

- Targeted resources to create more timely access in high-need areas
  - Reserve urgent or same-day GP slots specifically in practices serving deprived communities, with staffing levels that reflect demand, including locum and part-time coverage to avoid bottlenecks.
  - Extend hours in the evenings and weekends in clinics where people struggle to take time off work, and pilot walk-in sessions in community venues where people already go for other services.
  - Support better triage so someone presenting with a non-urgent issue isn’t forced into a long wait, yet those with urgent needs aren’t left waiting.

- Interpreters and language support as a guaranteed part of care
  - Guarantee access to qualified interpreters for all GP, nurse, and mental health consultations, including video and telephone options, with interpreters available for routine follow-ups.
  - Provide translated information on services, how to book appointments, and what to expect from care pathways in multiple languages commonly spoken in the local area.
  - Use bilingual staff wherever possible, and ensure interpreters are treated as part of the care team, not as an add-on.

- Culturally competent staff and outreach
  - Invest in ongoing, mandatory cultural competence training for all front-line staff and clinicians to understand different health beliefs, stigma, and expectations around care.
  - Recruit and retain staff from diverse backgrounds and establish community link workers or “care navigators” who understand local cultural nuances and can help people through the system.
  - Forge formal partnerships with community organisations, faith groups and schools to raise awareness of services and to help people know where to go when they need help.
  - Run targeted outreach sessions in venues used by migrant and marginalised groups, with drop-in clinics to discuss symptoms, signposting, and how to access mental health support.

- Proactive, accessible outreach and information channels
  - Deploy mobile health clinics or pop-up services in neighbourhood hubs, libraries, and housing estates with high deprivation, so people don’t have to travel far for initial assessments.
  - Provide clear, jargon-free information about what services exist and how to access them, including what to do in a mental health crisis, and make this information available in multiple languages and formats (video, audio, paper).
  - Ensure easy access to appointment booking by phone with reasonable call-back times and by preserving a simple online pathway for those who can use it.

- Integrated care and streamlined pathways
  - Improve integration between primary care, community health services, and mental health teams so a patient can move smoothly between services with a single care plan.
  - Expand same-day referrals from GP to mental health services where appropriate, so someone presenting with early anxiety or depression can start support quickly rather than waiting weeks.
  - Increase capacity in community-based mental health teams and IAPT, with special attention to culturally appropriate therapies and language-accessible options.

- Data, accountability and continuous improvement
  - Collect and publish data on wait times, access by ethnicity, language, and deprivation, and use this data to adjust resource allocation in real time.
  - Set local targets aligned with national goals and review progress at least quarterly, with feedback loops to communities so people can see what’s improving.

In practice, these changes would translate into fewer missed opportunities for early help, less time wasted on navigating a complicated system, and better outcomes for families who currently feel left behind. I’m glad this issue is being prioritised, and I’d like to see the government commit to the concrete actions above with clear funding and local implementation plans. If done well, this could strengthen trust in services, encourage earlier help-seeking, and reduce crises later on.

Overall, timely access should be seen not as a nice-to-have, but as a core part of fair and effective healthcare. Given the diverse and sometimes vulnerable makeup of our communities, targeted resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff and proactive outreach are essential to truly close the access gaps I’ve witnessed and heard about from others in my area.

I understand the aim to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I’m not persuaded that simply expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will deliver quicker, more reliable access in my area. In practice, the delay isn’t only about having more qualified people at the end of the pipeline; it’s about how services are organised on the ground today, and how we protect continuity of care for people who have multiple long‑standing health needs.

First, the biggest immediate win would be to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable conditions. I’m 65+ and my family includes someone with diabetes and another with heart and memory health concerns. Ten‑minute slots do not suffice when you’re trying to review multiple medications, assess new symptoms, and consider how an issue interacts with long‑standing problems. Longer, booked appointments with the same clinician where possible would likely reduce repeat visits, cut unnecessary trips to urgent care, and prevent deterioration that leads to hospital admissions. In a local practice I’ve used, when the usual GP was unavailable, new patients were allocated to a rotation; the result was fragmented care and repeated explanations of history at every visit.

Second, we must recognise that the current shortage isn’t solved quickly by more trainees alone. Training and apprenticeships are essential for the long term, but these workforce gains take years to materialise and must be matched by retention and sensible deployment. We need robust supervision and mentoring for those new to practice, and we should offer targeted return‑to‑practice paths that address real‑world pressures, not just theoretical knowledge. In the interim, I’d rather see incentives to keep experienced GPs, nurses and mental health professionals in post, with better workload management, flexible rosters, and adequate support staff so the front line isn’t constantly stretched.

Third, mental health and community services require urgent attention. In our area, there are weeks of waiting for talking therapies, and the most accessible crisis support is fragmented and distant. Patients in crisis cannot be left waiting while new training programmes slowly take effect. We should accelerate recruitment for community mental health teams, offer faster access through reliable triage, and fund alternatives that work in the short term—such as expanding the role of well‑supervised nurse prescribers and psychological wellbeing practitioners, while ensuring clear care plans and escalation routes so people aren’t bounced between services.

Fourth, we must ensure equitable access and avoid digital exclusion. Many older people struggle with online booking or telehealth, yet some may find in‑person consultations essential. Any plan that relies on high‑tech triage or online access must include a genuinely accessible option for those who prefer or need to travel to a GP or clinic and be able to be seen promptly by the same clinician where possible.

Specific steps I’d like to see include: (1) protected, longer appointment slots for complex cases, with reliable continuity of care; (2) immediate investment in practice‑level staffing and support roles (nurses, pharmacists, care coordinators) to free GPs for appropriate cases; (3) a fast‑track, well‑supported return‑to‑practice pathway with adequate supervision rather than ad hoc placements; (4) a strengthened, faster pathway into community mental health and talking therapies with clear referral choices and close monitoring; and (5) robust, local workforce planning that addresses rural and urban disparities so access isn’t worse in one part of the county.

If the policy focuses on expansion of training alone, we risk waiting longer for actual improvements in access and continuity. What matters most to patients like me is steady, predictable access to the same clinician, longer appointments when needed, and genuinely coordinated care across GP, community and mental health services. That would deliver better outcomes today while we build the workforce for tomorrow.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a live issue in our area. I’ve heard and seen how the pressure on primary and community teams can ripple through the system: more patients with complex needs, longer waits for welfare and mental health support, and patients repeatedly returning with the same issues because they can’t get a timely, appropriate response. I want to see changes that are practical, well funded and sustainable, not quick fixes that just shift the burden around. My view is that a combination of workforce renewal, expanded multidisciplinary care and patient‑centred scheduling is needed to improve access for everyone.

- Strengthen the workforce with targeted recruitment and better conditions
  - Invest in targeted recruitment campaigns and international hiring where appropriate, with clear settlement and induction support so recruits can contribute quickly and feel welcomed. This should be paired with return‑to‑practice pathways and streamlined credentialing to avoid long delays for competent professionals.
  - Improve pay, pensions and long‑term career progression for GPs, nurses and allied health staff, plus reliable locum cover so practices aren’t forced into unsafe or inefficient rates of workload. Flexible working patterns – such as shift sharing, part‑time routes, and predictable on‑call rosters – can help recruit and retain staff who might otherwise leave the profession.
  - Prioritise wellbeing and mental health support for staff, including easy access to occupational health and confidential counselling. When the workforce feels supported and rested, the quality of patient care improves and staff stay longer in their posts.
  - In practice terms, our local surgeries could benefit from a small but steady inflow of new clinicians and more stable teams. For example, practices piloting flexible rotas or longer‑term GP retention schemes in nearby areas have reported better morale and fewer gaps in cover, which translates into more available appointments for patients.

- Expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care and free GPs for complex cases
  - Systematically extend multidisciplinary teams (MDTs) within primary care and community hubs to include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates. These professionals can manage routine follow‑ups, medicines reviews, chronic disease management and minor injuries, leaving GPs to concentrate on complex, high‑risk cases.
  - Pharmacist‑led medicines optimisation and minor‑ailment clinics can reduce inappropriate calls and medication errors, while physiotherapists and paraprofessional first‑contact clinicians can triage and treat common musculoskeletal and other non‑urgent concerns. In other areas, pilots with expanded MDTs have shown a reduction in GP workload and faster access for patients with routine needs.
  - It’s important these teams work in true collaboration with GPs and community nurses, sharing records and care plans so patients aren’t shuffled between services. If done well, patients will experience more consistent care and shorter waits for the right person to respond.

- Protect continuity of care and invest in longer appointments for complex or vulnerable patients
  - For patients with chronic illness, mental health conditions or social vulnerabilities, continuity matters. Assigning patients to a named clinician where possible and maintaining a predictable contact path helps build knowledge of the patient’s history and reduces repeated, unnecessary visits.
  - Where appropriate, offer longer appointment slots (20–30 minutes for complex cases) to improve diagnostic clarity, care planning and adherence. Longer slots may feel like a luxury in a busy system, but they prevent repeated trips and miscommunication, ultimately saving time and improving outcomes.
  - Reconfiguring appointment scheduling to reserve blocks for complex cases and ensuring that triage does not automatically force move patients to new clinicians helps maintain trust and reduces fragmentation.

- Realistic implementation with clear measures
  - Roll out should be phased, with pilots in areas experiencing the greatest access pressures, and with robust metrics: wait times for routine and urgent care, patient and staff satisfaction, number of MDT patients managed in primary care, and rates of avoidable hospital admissions.
  - Funding must be ring‑fenced for workforce expansion, MDT integration and longer appointment times. Training and supervision for new roles (e.g., physician associates, pharmacists in primary care) are essential to ensure quality and safety.
  - Equity considerations are crucial: rural and underserved communities must not be last in line for these improvements. Transport, digital access and language needs should be factored into all planning so improvements are felt widely, not just in the easiest areas to reform.

In summary, timely access will improve if we grow and stabilise the workforce, extend the reach of multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care, and safeguard continuity and appropriate appointment lengths for those with the most complex needs. These changes must be well funded, well coordinated and evaluated so we learn and adapt as they roll out. I’m hopeful that with proper planning and commitment at local and national levels, we can deliver faster, safer and more compassionate care for everyone in our community.

As an organisation representing residents across England, we strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The key step is to guarantee evening and weekend clinics along with guaranteed same-day urgent slots. This would particularly help working people, carers and those with non‑emergency but pressing needs.

In practice, many residents struggle to secure weekday appointments without taking time off. For example, in our area a patient with persistent respiratory symptoms waited two weeks for a routine GP slot; another person seeking urgent mental health support faced delays that aggravated anxiety. Evening clinics (for example until 8pm on two weekdays) and a Saturday urgent slot would allow people to be seen in a timely, compassionate way without compromising work or family commitments. A robust same-day urgent slot policy, with clear triage to mental health crises, would prevent deterioration and reduce hospital admissions.

We also urge better coordination between primary care, community nursing and CCGs, plus transparent booking systems so people know when slots are available. With predictable, extended hours and urgent access pathways, health services stay close to home where families live.

Agree. The most impactful changes would be to expand community mental health teams, invest in early intervention, strengthen crisis response, and widen access to talking therapies so people don’t wait months for help. In my area a GP referral for anxiety or depressive symptoms can lead to a multi‑week wait before any talking therapy is offered, and urgent cases still feel uncertain. A friend faced about a two‑month delay for CAMHS input after a referral, which added to distress and meant relying on charity helplines that aren’t a long‑term solution. 

Concrete steps I’d welcome: scale up community mental health teams with dedicated early‑intervention slots (including young adults and first-episode psychosis teams) and guarantee triage within days and initial assessments within 2–4 weeks. fund 24/7 crisis response with mobile teams and rapid home-based assessments to avoid unnecessary hospital visits. expand capacity for talking therapies (CBT, ACT, IPT, other evidence‑based options) with flexible hours, group programmes, and online options; ensure referrals are followed through quickly. integrate mental health more closely with GP services via co‑located staff, shared records, and mental health‑trained practitioners in primary care. sustained investment and workforce planning will help parity with physical health and reduce avoidable waits.

Access to GP and community health and mental health services in Wales, including my area, has been uneven, especially outside core hours. I welcome changes to grow and retain primary care staff through targeted recruitment and international hiring, with incentives, pay improvements, flexible working, and wellbeing support. Our demographics mean we need a robust pipeline: support overseas GP placements, return-to-practice courses for recently qualified clinicians, and targeted incentives for practice nurses and district nurses. Flexible rotas, shorter shifts with proper breaks, and protected admin time would reduce burnout and help teams stay stable. Wellbeing packages, supervision, and peer support help staff deliver safer care.

On access, I want NHS111 and clinical triage to be sharper: better nurse-led triage, clearer pathways to same-day slots, and direct booking into GP, mental health, or community services via a single, user-friendly system. Reducing duplication through care navigation and shared records across GP, community teams and pharmacies would simplify patient flow. In practice, this would mean same-day mental health assessments, faster referrals to community care, and predictable appointment windows instead of repeated calls. These changes would bring quicker, safer care for families such as mine.

From our organisation’s perspective, improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is vital. However, I am not convinced that expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates) to handle routine cases will deliver the promised speed or safety gains. In practice, routine management becomes a maze of handovers between roles, which often slows decision-making and confuses patients about who is ultimately coordinating care. In our area we’ve seen pilots where simple musculoskeletal issues are routed to a physio or pharmacist, yet patients report delays when escalation to a GP is needed or when a prescription or adjustment requires GP input. For individuals with complex needs—polypharmacy, co-morbid depression or anxiety, social factors—the risk of fragmented care and missed signals increases if responsibility is too diffusely shared (as if that will ever happen). There is also potential for inequity: not every practice can sustain a full MDT, which could widen gaps between communities.

If MDTs are pursued, they must be under tight governance: integrated electronic records, clearly defined roles and escalation pathways, guaranteed GP oversight, and dedicated funding for co-ordination and admin time. Without that, the benefit to timely access will be limited. I would prioritise bolstering GP capacity and strengthening community mental health teams, with MDTs deployed only as a well-governed supplement rather than a default approach.
